question: A procurement officer will ask Claude to summarise an uploaded framework agreement into about forty points, and a colleague will have to spot-check that summary against the agreement in fifteen minutes. What should she build into the request to make that check practical?
options: A) Ask for each point to name the clause of the agreement it came from, so the colleague can go straight to that clause and compare.
B) Ask for the points to be ordered by how commercially important each one is, so the colleague starts with the points that matter most.
C) Ask for the summary to be kept to short single sentences, so the colleague can read the whole of it well inside the fifteen minutes.
D) Ask for a confidence rating beside each point, so the colleague can concentrate the checking effort on the points rated least certain.
correct_answers: A) Ask for each point to name the clause of the agreement it came from, so the colleague can go straight to that clause and compare.
explanations: Correct. Tying each point to its clause turns verification into a direct comparison at source, which is the only step that shows whether the agreement was represented accurately, and it fits the time available.
Importance ordering helps the colleague choose what to look at, but it does not help him find the corresponding clause in a long agreement, which is where the fifteen minutes would actually be spent.
Brevity makes the summary quicker to read but no quicker to verify. The colleague can read every point and still be unable to locate the clause each one is supposed to rest on.
A self-declared confidence rating is not a reliable guide to which points are wrong, and it can misdirect the check by giving high confidence to a point that was misread from the agreement.
